note: A ratio, not a count. Absolute survivor counts rise with every
line added -- new code means new mutants, so a healthy change
with good tests would trip an absolute ratchet. The score below
is killed / (killed + survived): it stays comparable as the
codebase grows and only moves when tests get better or worse.
Not every survivor is a gap. About a quarter only change a log
or error message, which nothing asserts on by design. Others are
equivalent: `if not mismatched` decides when the read-back loop
exits, not what it returns, so killing it would mean asserting on
timing -- a worse test than the mutant is a risk.
Mutants with no covering test are excluded from the score rather
than counted as failures: the tests that drive a module through a
real subprocess load the original source, so a mutation run says
nothing about what they cover. See
docs/decisions/0005-mutation-testing-scope.md.
0.72 -> 0.63 (2026-08-16). THE SCORE FELL AND THE SUITE GOT
BETTER. Both are true, and the second causes the first.
The old floor was measured when 677 mutants counted as
not_covered, because cli, session and process were reachable only
through a subprocess. tests/test_lifecycle.py and
tests/test_process.py now drive them in process, and the launcher
moved into the package with tests/test_launcher.py behind it. That
took not_covered from 677 to 81 -- and every mutant that stops
being 'not covered' starts being judged. Four modules that had
been excluded from the denominator entirely are now in it,
carrying the survivors that were always there and were simply not
being counted.
So this is not a relaxed floor, it is the first floor measured
against the whole runtime. Raising it means killing survivors in
code that was invisible to this gate until now, which is the
useful direction: the survivors are findable rather than
structurally out of reach.

why_not_comparable: 677 of those 2066 mutants were never judged. The 0.728 describes
the third of the runtime that in-process tests reached at the

floor_note: The gate is min_score - tolerance = 0.63. That is the number that
matters: the score may not fall below it. min_score itself is set
at the measured 0.643 rounded down, so the policy neither fails
nor nags on the run it was recorded from -- a baseline that prints
'raise me' on every CI run teaches people to ignore it.
